title: Constitution Quiz (Indian Constitution)

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Preamble of the Indian Constitution as amended by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976:

Statement 1: The words 'SOCIALIST' and 'SECULAR' were inserted into the description of the Republic.
Statement 2: The phrase 'Unity of the Nation' was substituted with 'unity and integrity of the Nation'.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: While Statement 1 is true, it is not the only change made by the 42nd Amendment; the integrity of the nation was also addressed.
Statement 2 is true, but the amendment also famously added the socialist and secular nature to the Preamble.
The 42nd Amendment of 1976 introduced three new words to the Preamble: 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity'.
Both statements accurately reflect the specific textual changes mandated by the Forty-second Amendment in 1976.

questions.hint: Recall the specific terminology added during the Emergency period amendments.

questions.question:
Regarding the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), consider the following statements based on the provided text:

Statement 1: It was established by the Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Act, 2014.
Statement 2: The Commission currently functions as the primary body for the appointment of Supreme Court Judges.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: The 99th Amendment did insert Article $124A$ to establish the NJAC, but the provided text notes that this amendment was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015.
The NJAC is not the current functioning body because the 99th Amendment was declared invalid by the Supreme Court in $AIR\ 2016\ SC\ 117$.
While the amendment exists in the legislative history, the footnote in the source material clearly states it has been struck down.
Statement 1 is a correct historical and legislative fact according to the provided footnotes in the Constitution's text.

questions.hint: Check the status of the 99th Amendment in the footnotes of the Union Judiciary chapter.

questions.question:
Which of the following is the correct chronological order of the following Constitutional Amendment Acts as mentioned in the text?

1. Constitution (One Hundredth Amendment) Act
2. Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act
3. Constitution (One Hundred and Third Amendment) Act
4. Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act

answerOptions.rationale: The 100th (Land Boundary Agreement) was in 2015, the 101st (GST) in 2016, the 103rd (EWS) in 2019, and the 106th (Women's Reservation) in 2023.
The Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh preceded the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax.
The 101st Amendment regarding GST occurred in 2016, which is before the 103rd Amendment of 2019.
This represents a reverse chronological order, starting from the most recent amendment in 2023.

questions.hint: The order follows the numerical sequence of the amendments from 2015 to 2023.

questions.question:
Match the following Articles with their respective subject matters as per the provided text:

(A) Article 243-I  (i) Special provisions for Delhi
(B) Article 239AA  (ii) Constitution of Finance Commission for Panchayats
(C) Article 279A   (iii) Goods and Services Tax Council
(D) Article 371A   (iv) Special provision for Nagaland

answerOptions.rationale: Article $243-I$ mandates state finance commissions, $239AA$ details Delhi's special status, $279A$ establishes the GST Council, and $371A$ provides special status to Nagaland.
Article $243-I$ is related to local bodies (Panchayats) rather than Union Territory administration (Delhi).
Article $279A$ is specifically for the GST Council, while Article $371A$ is part of the special provisions for certain states.
This pairing incorrectly associates Nagaland with Article $243-I$ and GST with Article $239AA$.

questions.hint: Look for the articles within the chapters on Panchayats, Union Territories, Finance, and Special Provisions.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council under Article 279A:

Statement 1: The Council shall recommend the date on which GST be levied on petroleum crude and high-speed diesel.
Statement 2: The Council has the authority to recommend special rates to raise additional resources during any natural calamity.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Statement 1 is correct, but the Council also has constitutional power regarding natural calamities as stated in Statement 2.
Statement 2 is correct, but Article $279A(5)$ also specifically mentions the Council's role in determining the start of tax on petroleum products.
Article $279A$ empowers the GST Council to handle both the inclusion of petroleum products and special rates for disaster resource mobilization.
Both statements accurately represent powers and duties of the GST Council as defined in the 101st Amendment.

questions.hint: Article 279A outlines the recommendations the Council can make for various goods and situations.

questions.question: According to Article 13 of the Constitution, which of the following is NOT included in the definition of 'law' for the purposes of that article?

answerOptions.text: Custom or usage having the force of law
answerOptions.rationale: Article $13(3)(a)$ explicitly states that 'law' includes any custom or usage having the force of law in the territory of India.
Ordinances are specifically listed in the inclusive definition of 'law' under Article $13(3)(a)$.
Article $13(4)$, inserted by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971, specifies that nothing in Article 13 applies to amendments made under Article 368.
Both notifications and bye-laws are explicitly included in the definition of 'law' under Article $13(3)(a)$.

questions.hint: Examine the specific clause added by the Twenty-fourth Amendment Act, 1971.

questions.question:
Regarding the administration of Jammu and Kashmir, consider the following statements based on Appendix II and III:

Statement 1: The Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019, superseded the 1954 Order.
Statement 2: As of August 6, 2019, all clauses of Article 370 have ceased to be operative.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is incorrect because the text of C.O. 273 states all clauses ceased to be operative 'except' for a specific modified version of the article.
Statement 2 is a trap; Article 370 was not entirely deleted but made inoperative except for one substituted clause.
Statement 2 contains a significant inaccuracy regarding the total cessation of Article 370 as described in Appendix III.
Statement 1 correctly identifies C.O. 272 as the order that superseded the previous 1954 framework.

questions.hint: Check the exact wording of the Declaration under Article 370(3) in Appendix III.

questions.question: In the context of Part IX (The Panchayats), who is constitutionally empowered to review the financial position of the Panchayats and make recommendations to the Governor?

answerOptions.text: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
answerOptions.rationale: While the CAG audits accounts, the specific duty of reviewing financial positions and recommendations belongs to the Finance Commission.

answerOptions.text: The Finance Commission constituted under Article 243-I
answerOptions.rationale: Article $243-I$ requires the Governor to constitute a Finance Commission at the expiration of every fifth year to review the financial position of Panchayats.

answerOptions.text: The Central Finance Commission under Article 280
answerOptions.rationale: Article 280 relates to the Union Finance Commission, whereas Article $243-I$ establishes a separate State-level commission for local bodies.
The Assembly makes laws for the commission, but it is the Commission itself that performs the review and makes recommendations.

questions.hint: Think of the specific body mandated to be formed every five years at the state level.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the powers of the Governor to promulgate Ordinances during the recess of the Legislature (Article 213):

Statement 1: The Governor can promulgate an Ordinance even if the Legislative Assembly is in session, provided the Legislative Council is not.
Statement 2: The Governor shall not, without instructions from the President, promulgate an Ordinance if a Bill containing the same provisions would have required previous sanction of the President.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Article 213 requires both Houses (if applicable) to be in recess; an Ordinance cannot be promulgated if the Assembly is in session.
Statement 2 correctly identifies one of the specific conditions under the Proviso to Article 213(1) where Presidential instruction is mandatory.
Statement 1 contradicts Article 213(1), which states the power exists only when the House or both Houses are NOT in session.
Statement 2 is a direct extract from the constitutional provisions governing the Governor's legislative powers.

questions.hint: Check the conditions in Article 213 regarding when the House(s) must be in recess and when the President must be involved.

questions.question: Which Constitutional Amendment substituted the phrase 'SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC' with 'SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC' in the Preamble?

answerOptions.rationale: The 1st Amendment dealt primarily with fundamental rights and the 9th Schedule, not the core description of the Republic in the Preamble.
The 7th Amendment focused on the reorganization of states and the abolition of Part A, B, and C state classifications.
Section 2 of the 42nd Amendment implemented this major change to the Preamble's opening declaration, effective from January 3, 1977.
The 44th Amendment sought to reverse many 42nd Amendment changes but did not remove 'Socialist' or 'Secular' from the Preamble.

questions.hint: This is often referred to as the 'Mini-Constitution' and was passed during the Emergency.

questions.question:
Regarding Article 19 (Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.), consider the following statements:

Statement 1: All citizens have the right to form co-operative societies.
Statement 2: The right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property remains a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(f).

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Statement 1 was added by the 97th Amendment. Statement 2 is incorrect because Article $19(1)(f)$ was omitted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
The fundamental right to property was abolished and moved to Article $300A$ as a legal right, not a fundamental right.
Statement 2 is factually incorrect according to the text and footnotes regarding the 44th Amendment.
Statement 1 is correct as the 97th Amendment inserted 'or co-operative societies' into Article $19(1)(c)$.

questions.hint: Check the footnotes for Article 19 and the history of the Right to Property.

questions.question: According to the Seventh Schedule, 'Preventive detention for reasons connected with the security of a State' falls under which List?

answerOptions.rationale: The Union List (Entry 9) covers preventive detention for reasons of Defence, Foreign Affairs, or the security of India.
The State List contains many local matters, but preventive detention is a shared or specific Union subject depending on the cause.
Entry 3 of the Concurrent List covers preventive detention for reasons connected with the security of a State or public order.
Preventive detention is specifically enumerated in the Lists, so it does not fall under residuary powers.

questions.hint: Differentiate between security of 'India' and security of a 'State' in the Seventh Schedule entries.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Attorney-General for India (Article 76):

Statement 1: The President appoints a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court.
Statement 2: In the performance of his duties, the Attorney-General shall have the right of audience in all courts in the territory of India.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Statement 1 is correct, but the Attorney-General also possesses the specific right of audience mentioned in Statement 2.
Statement 2 is correct, but Article 76(1) also specifies the qualifications required for the appointment.
Both statements are directly supported by clauses (1) and (3) of Article 76.
Both statements accurately represent the constitutional provisions for the office of the Attorney-General.

questions.hint: Article 76 describes both the appointment qualifications and the privileges of the office.

questions.question: Which of the following bodies/individuals has the 'Duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance' as per Article 355?

answerOptions.rationale: While the President issues proclamations, Article 355 specifically names 'The Union' as the entity having this duty.
Article 355 explicitly states it shall be the duty of the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance.
The Governor represents the State and may report failures, but the duty of protection lies with the Union.
Parliament has powers to legislate during emergencies, but the specific duty under Article 355 is assigned to the Union.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 368 (Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution):

Statement 1: An amendment seeking to change the representation of States in Parliament requires ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States.
Statement 2: No Constitutional Amendment shall be called in question in any court on any ground.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Statement 1 is correct under the Proviso to Article $368(2)$. Statement 2 is incorrect because the text notes that clause (4) and (5), which tried to bar judicial review, were declared invalid by the Supreme Court in the Minerva Mills case.
Statement 2 refers to clauses that were struck down by the Supreme Court as per the footnotes in the document.
Statement 2 is invalid due to the judicial ruling in $Minerva\ Mills\ vs.\ Union\ of\ India$.
Statement 1 is a correct procedural requirement for amending certain entrenched provisions of the Constitution.

questions.hint: Check the footnotes for Article 368 regarding the Minerva Mills case and the Proviso to clause (2).

questions.question: The 'Administrative Tribunals' were provided for in the Constitution through which Part, as mentioned in the text?

answerOptions.rationale: Part XIV deals with Services under the Union and States, not specifically with tribunals.
Part $XIVA$ (Articles $323A$ and $323B$) was inserted to provide for the establishment of administrative and other tribunals.

Part XVI contains Special Provisions Relating to Certain Classes like SCs and STs.

answerOptions.rationale: The list of articles for Part XVI shows Article $330A$ was inserted by the 106th Amendment for the reservation of seats for women in the House of the People.
Article $342A$ relates to socially and educationally backward classes and was part of earlier amendments (102nd/105th).
Article $246A$ was inserted by the 101st Amendment to enable the levy of GST.
Article $21A$, the Right to Education, was added much earlier by the 86th Amendment.

questions.hint: Search Part XVI for an article with a letter suffix recently added for women's representation.

questions.question: Which article provides for the 'Authoritative text in the Hindi language' of the Constitution?

answerOptions.rationale: Article 343 declares Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language, but doesn't specify the authoritative text of the Constitution.
Article 351 provides a directive for the development of the Hindi language.
Article $394A$, inserted by the 58th Amendment in 1987, requires the President to publish the authoritative translation of the Constitution in Hindi.
Article 395 is the final article of the Constitution and deals with the repeal of previous colonial acts.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Ninth Schedule:

Statement 1: Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule are immune from challenge on the ground of inconsistency with Part III rights.
Statement 2: The Ninth Schedule was added to the Constitution by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Both statements are correct; Statement 2 is the historical origin, and Statement 1 is the core function described in Article $31B$.
While Statement 2 is correct, the immunity described in Statement 1 is the defining characteristic of the Ninth Schedule.

questions.question:

While citizenship and Rajya Sabha eligibility are correct, the age threshold is specifically 35 years.

questions.question: Regarding the term of the Governor's office, which of the following is true according to the provided text?

answerOptions.text: The Governor has a fixed term of five years and cannot be removed before its completion.
answerOptions.rationale: While a five-year term is mentioned, it is explicitly subject to the pleasure of the President, meaning it is not fixed.

answerOptions.text: A Governor can hold office beyond five years until a successor assumes charge.
answerOptions.rationale: The source states that a Governor can continue in office even after the five-year term expires until the successor takes over.

answerOptions.text: The Governor submits their resignation letter to the Chief Justice of the state High Court.
answerOptions.rationale: Resignation must be addressed to the President of India, not the Chief Justice of the High Court.

questions.question:

questions.hint: Check the conditions of the Governor's office regarding legislative membership.

questions.question: Which commission/committee suggested that the Governor should be a 'detached figure without intense political links'?

answerOptions.rationale: The ARC focused on general administration rather than this specific definition of the Governor's persona.
This committee was focused on state autonomy but is not credited with this specific 'detached figure' quote in the source.
The source identifies the Sarkaria Commission as the body that suggested the Governor be an eminent person from outside the state and a detached figure.
While important, the specific phrasing provided in the Prelims question refers to the 1983 commission.

answerOptions.text: The Governor presides over the session personally.

answerOptions.text: The Governor must dissolve the assembly immediately.

answerOptions.text: The Chief Justice of the High Court presides over the session.

questions.question: According to the source, what is the role of the Governor in the appointment of High Court judges?

questions.question: Under what condition can the Governor be arrested or imprisoned during their term of office?

answerOptions.rationale: The Governor enjoys absolute immunity from arrest or imprisonment while in office.

questions.question: Which official's remuneration is determined by the Governor?

title: Constitutional Quiz (Practice Questions - Historical Underpinnings)

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Regulating Act of $1773$:
1. It was the $1^{st}$ step by the British Government to regulate the East India Company's affairs.
2. It established the foundations for a decentralized administrative setup in India.
3. It recognized the political and administrative functions of the Company.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: The Act marked the initial move toward government control and recognized specific Company functions, but it actually laid the foundation for centralized, not decentralized, administration.
While the Act initiated regulation and recognized functions, statement 2 is incorrect because the Act aimed at centralization rather than decentralization.
This option incorrectly includes the idea of decentralization, which contradicts the Act's role in establishing a centralized administrative structure.
This ignores the critical historical fact that the $1773$ Act was the very first legislative step taken by the British Government to oversee the Company.

questions.hint: Think about whether the British aimed to consolidate power in one place or spread it across the presidencies.

questions.question:
Regarding the Charter Act of $1813$, consider the following statements:
1. It completely abolished the trade monopoly of the East India Company in India.
2. It explicitly asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over Company territories.
3. It barred Christian missionaries from entering India for the purpose of enlightenment.

Which of the statements is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: The Act abolished the trade monopoly and asserted Crown sovereignty while actually allowing, rather than barring, Christian missionaries.
While the Act did assert sovereignty, the source material specifically identifies only the abolition of the trade monopoly as the primary feature among these options.
This is incorrect because the Act promoted the entry of missionaries rather than preventing them from coming to India.
This option fails to recognize the major economic shift of ending the trade monopoly and incorrectly suggests a ban on missionaries.

questions.hint: One of these statements regarding the religious policy of the British is the exact opposite of what actually occurred.

questions.question: Which specific Act was responsible for the final step towards centralization in British India?

answerOptions.rationale: This Act completed the centralization process by elevating the Governor-General of Bengal to the status of Governor-General of India.
While this Act laid the foundations of centralization, it was the beginning of the process rather than the final step.
This Act focused more on trade monopoly and sovereignty rather than finalizing the internal administrative hierarchy of India.
This was the last of the Charter Acts and focused on separating legislative and executive functions rather than initiating the final stage of centralization.

questions.hint: Look for the Act that expanded the jurisdiction of the Governor-General from a presidency to the entire country.

questions.question: The 'Act of Settlement' of $1781$ was enacted primarily to:

answerOptions.text: Exempt the Governor-General and Council from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction for official acts.
answerOptions.rationale: This Act sought to rectify the defects of the $1773$ Act by protecting the executive's official actions from judicial interference.

answerOptions.text: Establish a Board of Control to manage the political affairs of the Company.
answerOptions.rationale: The management of political affairs through a Board of Control was a feature of the Pitt's India Act of $1784$.

answerOptions.text: Empower the Supreme Court to frame regulations for the Provincial Courts.
answerOptions.rationale: The Act actually aimed to define boundaries, and the source material indicates the Supreme Court was not given this specific power over provincial regulations.

answerOptions.text: Abolish the trade monopoly of the East India Company.
answerOptions.rationale: The trade monopoly remained intact until the later Charter Acts of the $19^{th}$ century.

questions.hint: Consider the need to reduce friction between the judiciary and the executive branch after $1773$.

questions.question: Which of the following legislative measures first distinguished the commercial and political functions of the East India Company?

answerOptions.rationale: This Act created a dual system of control by separating the commercial interests from the political and administrative functions.
This Act was the first to recognize the Company's functions but did not yet provide a clear structural distinction between commercial and political roles.
This Act was more concerned with judicial jurisdiction and rectifying administrative conflicts than with functional separation.
This Act followed the Pitt's India Act and continued its principles but was not the origin of the functional distinction.

questions.hint: Identify the Act that introduced a 'Board of Control' specifically for political matters.

questions.question: Consider the features of the Regulating Act of $1773$. Which of the following was NOT a provision of this Act?

answerOptions.text: Establishment of a Board of Control for managing political affairs.
answerOptions.rationale: The Board of Control was established by the Pitt's India Act of $1784$, not the Regulating Act of $1773$.

answerOptions.text: Provision for the establishment of a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
answerOptions.rationale: This was a core feature of the $1773$ Act, leading to the court's actual creation in $1774$.

answerOptions.text: Creation of an executive council for the Governor-General of Bengal.
answerOptions.rationale: The Act established a council of four to assist the Governor-General of Bengal in his duties.

answerOptions.text: Subordination of the Bombay and Madras presidencies to Bengal.
answerOptions.rationale: One of the centralizing features of this Act was making the other two presidencies answerable to the Governor-General of Bengal.

questions.hint: One of these features belongs to an Act passed approximately a decade after $1773$.

questions.question:
Arrange the following historical acts in correct chronological order:
1. Pitt's India Act
2. Charter Act of $1833$
3. Regulating Act
4. Act of Settlement

answerOptions.rationale: The Regulating Act was passed in $1773$, followed by the Act of Settlement in $1781$, Pitt's India Act in $1784$, and the Charter Act in $1833$.
This order incorrectly places Pitt's India Act ($1784$) before the Act of Settlement ($1781$).
This sequence wrongly suggests that Pitt's India Act was the earliest legislative measure among those listed.
The Act of Settlement was an amendment to the Regulating Act and therefore must come after it in chronology.

questions.hint: The first step in regulation was in $1773$, while the major centralization shift occurred in the $19^{th}$ century.

questions.question:
Regarding the Indian Councils Act of $1892$, which of the following statements is/are true?
1. It provided for the direct use of the word 'election' in the Act.
2. It made a limited and indirect provision for using election to fill non-official seats.

answerOptions.rationale: The Act introduced the principle of election indirectly but carefully avoided using the specific word 'election' within the text of the Act.
The source explicitly states that the Act did not use the word 'election' directly, despite introducing the process.
These statements are contradictory; the Act provided for the process of election while simultaneously omitting the specific terminology.
Statement 2 is a historically accurate description of how the representation was increased under the $1892$ Act.

questions.hint: This Act introduced the concept of voting without actually naming it.

questions.question:
Match the following Acts with their respective features:
I. Regulating Act $1773$
II. Charter Act $1853$
III. Indian Councils Act $1861$
IV. Charter Act $1833$

A. Separated Legislative and Executive functions
B. Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India
C. Established Supreme Court at Calcutta
D. Provided for Legislative Council for Punjab

answerOptions.rationale: The $1773$ Act set up the Supreme Court; the $1853$ Act separated council functions; the $1861$ Act established provincial councils (like Punjab); and the $1833$ Act changed the GG title.
This incorrectly associates the separation of functions with $1833$ and the title change with $1853$.
This match wrongly attributes the title of Governor-General of India to the $1773$ Act, which only created the Governor-General of Bengal.
This sequence fails to correctly pair the foundational acts with their most significant constitutional outcomes.

questions.hint: Recall that the title 'Governor-General of India' was part of the final step of centralization.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the Charter Act of $1853$?

answerOptions.text: It was the last of the series of Charter Acts passed by the British Parliament.
answerOptions.rationale: The $1853$ Act concluded the era of Charter Acts before the Company's rule was significantly altered following the $1857$ uprising.

answerOptions.text: It combined the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's council.
answerOptions.rationale: In reality, the $1853$ Act took the step of separating these two functions for the first time.

answerOptions.text: It made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India.
answerOptions.rationale: This significant administrative change was actually enacted by the Charter Act of $1833$.

answerOptions.text: It was the first step taken by the British Government to regulate the Company's affairs.
answerOptions.rationale: This description applies to the Regulating Act of $1773$, not the $1853$ Charter Act.

questions.hint: This Act is notable for being the final one in its specific legal category.

questions.question: The Supreme Court at Calcutta, established in $1774$, owed its legal existence to which Act?

answerOptions.rationale: The Regulating Act provided the statutory authority for the creation of the Supreme Court, which was then formally established the following year.
The $1781$ Act was passed to modify and clarify the jurisdiction of the already existing Supreme Court.
This Act focused on political control and the dual system, rather than the initial establishment of the judiciary.
The court was established decades before the $1793$ Act was passed.

questions.hint: Consider the very first constitutional step taken by the British Parliament regarding India.

questions.question: In the context of the Indian Councils Act of $1861$, which of the following was a key feature according to the provided historical text?

answerOptions.text: The establishment of a Legislative Council for Punjab.
answerOptions.rationale: The $1861$ Act expanded the legislative apparatus, including the provision for councils in provinces like Punjab.

answerOptions.text: The introduction of the Portfolio system.
answerOptions.rationale: While historically true, the source material explicitly suggests that the Act 'rejected' or did not provide for it in its correct answer logic (Q8).

answerOptions.text: The complete centralization of legislative power.
answerOptions.rationale: The Act actually initiated a tendency toward decentralization, moving away from the extreme centralization of $1833$.

answerOptions.text: The exclusion of Indians from the law-making process.
answerOptions.rationale: The Act was significant for starting to associate Indians with the law-making process, not excluding them.

questions.hint: This Act dealt with the expansion of legislative councils to the provinces.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Act of Settlement ($1781$):
1. It allowed the Supreme Court to have jurisdiction over the official actions of the Governor-General.
2. It was passed to rectify the defects of the Regulating Act of $1773$.

Which of the statements is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: The Act was designed to fix $1773$ defects by specifically exempting (not including) the Governor-General's official acts from the court's jurisdiction.
This is incorrect because the primary purpose of the Act was to remove the Governor-General from such jurisdiction.
Statement 1 is false because it contradicts the Act's main goal of exempting the executive from the court.
Statement 2 is accurate as the $1781$ Act is formally known as the Amending Act to fix the $1773$ Regulating Act.

questions.hint: One statement accurately describes the Act's purpose, while the other describes a power it actually sought to limit.

questions.question: The Governor-General of Bengal's executive council was originally comprised of how many members under the Regulating Act of $1773$?

answerOptions.rationale: The $1773$ Act created an executive council consisting of four members to assist the Governor-General.
Three was the number of members in later versions or different councils, but the original $1773$ council had four.
This number is associated with the legislative additions in the $1853$ Act, not the original $1773$ executive council.
The council was larger than two to ensure a broader administrative oversight of the Company's affairs.

questions.hint: This number is one more than three.

questions.question: Which Act first mandated that the governors of Bombay and Madras were subordinate to the Governor-General of Bengal?

answerOptions.rationale: This was the first step toward a unified central authority in India, placing the other presidencies under Bengal's control.
While it strengthened control, the subordination was legally established earlier in $1773$.
This Act focused more on trade and sovereignty rather than the basic structural relationship between the presidencies.
By $1861$, the system was actually beginning to move back toward decentralization.

questions.hint: It was the same Act that created the post of Governor-General of Bengal.

questions.question: What was the primary role of the 'Board of Control' established by the Pitt's India Act of $1784$?

answerOptions.rationale: The Board of Control was specifically designed to oversee the political and military government of the Company.
Commercial functions remained under the control of the Court of Directors, creating a dual system of governance.

answerOptions.text: Framing regulations for the Supreme Court
answerOptions.rationale: The Board of Control was an executive/political body and did not possess the authority to regulate the Supreme Court's internal procedures.
The entry of missionaries was governed by the Charter Act of $1813$, not by the Board of Control in $1784$.

questions.hint: Think about the distinction made between money-making and governing.

questions.question:
Consider the chronological sequence of these administrative changes:
1. Recognition of political functions of the EIC.
2. Assertion of British Crown sovereignty.
3. Separation of legislative and executive functions.
4. Provision for indirect elections.

answerOptions.rationale: Political functions were recognized in $1773$, sovereignty asserted in $1813$, functions separated in $1853$, and indirect elections provided in $1892$.
Sovereignty was asserted in $1813$, which is much later than the initial recognition of political functions in $1773$.
The separation of legislative and executive functions ($1853$) occurred after the assertion of Crown sovereignty ($1813$).
The provision for indirect elections ($1892$) was one of the last major acts of the $19^{th}$ century, following the $1853$ changes.

questions.hint: The order follows the natural progression from the $18^{th}$ century to the late $19^{th}$ century.

questions.question: The Charter Act of $1813$ is significant for which of the following reasons?

answerOptions.text: It allowed Christian missionaries to come to India to enlighten the people.
answerOptions.rationale: The Act opened the door for religious and educational activities by allowing missionaries to operate in India.

answerOptions.text: It made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India.
answerOptions.rationale: This change happened in $1833$, twenty years after the $1813$ Act.

answerOptions.text: It created the first Supreme Court in Calcutta.
answerOptions.rationale: The Supreme Court was established by the Regulating Act of $1773$.

answerOptions.text: It ended the political functions of the East India Company.
answerOptions.rationale: The Company's political functions continued long after $1813$, only ending after the $1857$ revolt.

questions.hint: This Act combined economic changes with social and religious openings.

questions.question: According to the Act of $1781$, the Supreme Court was specifically restricted from interfering in:

answerOptions.text: Acts done by the Governor-General and Council in their official capacity.
answerOptions.rationale: This exemption was a key feature of the Act of Settlement to ensure the executive could function without legal deadlock.

answerOptions.text: Commercial disputes involving the Company's trade.
answerOptions.rationale: The restriction was primarily political/administrative rather than a general ban on commercial litigation.

answerOptions.text: The appointment of the Board of Control.
answerOptions.rationale: The Board of Control didn't exist until $1784$; the $1781$ Act couldn't restrict something not yet established.

answerOptions.text: The legislative functions of the Governor-General of India.
answerOptions.rationale: The title 'Governor-General of India' did not exist in $1781$; he was still the Governor-General of Bengal.

questions.hint: The goal was to protect the 'official capacity' of the high-ranking administrators.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the nature of the Indian Councils Act of $1892$ regarding the representation of people?

answerOptions.text: It made a limited and indirect provision for elections.
answerOptions.rationale: The Act introduced the elective principle for the first time in a restricted, indirect manner.

answerOptions.text: It introduced a system of direct adult franchise.
answerOptions.rationale: Direct franchise and universal voting were developments that occurred much later in Indian constitutional history.

answerOptions.text: It prohibited the use of elections for non-official seats.
answerOptions.rationale: On the contrary, the Act was the first to allow for an elective element in filling non-official positions.

answerOptions.text: It officially established the word 'election' in the constitutional lexicon.
answerOptions.rationale: While it allowed for the process, the Act notoriously avoided using the actual word 'election'.

questions.hint: Think of a process that is present in practice but not mentioned by name in the legal text.

title: Amendment Quiz (Amendment Procedure + Basic Structure)

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the initiation of a Constitutional Amendment Bill:
1. The bill can be introduced in either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha.
2. Prior recommendation of the President is mandatory for introducing the bill.
3. The bill can be introduced only by a Minister of the Union Cabinet.

answerOptions.rationale: The bill can be initiated in either House of Parliament and does not require prior presidential permission or restriction to ministers; it can be introduced by private members.
This incorrectly assumes that the President's prior permission is required, which is not the case for Constitutional Amendment Bills.
This suggests both presidential permission is needed and private members are excluded, both of which are incorrect according to the amendment procedure.
This option fails to account for the fact that neither presidential recommendation nor exclusive ministerial introduction is required by Article 368.

questions.hint: Check the source material for rules regarding prior permission and the status of private members.

questions.question:
Regarding the passage of a Constitutional Amendment Bill, consider the following statements:
1. In case of a deadlock between the two Houses, the President can summon a joint sitting.
2. The bill must be passed in each House by a special majority separately.

answerOptions.rationale: There is no provision for a joint sitting for Constitutional Amendment Bills; they must be passed by both Houses individually.
Each House must pass the bill separately using the special majority required under Article 368, with no option for a joint sitting.
While the requirement for separate special majorities is true, the provision for a joint sitting is explicitly absent for constitutional amendments.
This incorrectly denies that the bill must be passed in each House by a special majority, which is a core requirement of Article 368.

questions.hint: Consider how disagreements between the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha are handled for this specific type of bill.

questions.question:
Arrange the following judicial and legislative events in correct chronological order:
1. Kesavananda Bharati case
2. Golak Nath case
3. Shankari Prasad case
4. 24th Amendment Act

answerOptions.rationale: The correct sequence is Shankari Prasad (1951), Golak Nath (1967), 24th Amendment (1971), and Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
This incorrectly places the 24th Amendment before the Golak Nath case, whereas the amendment was actually a response to that case.
This incorrectly starts with the Golak Nath case (1967), missing the earlier Shankari Prasad case (1951).
This sequence wrongly suggests that the Kesavananda Bharati case occurred before the 24th Amendment Act.

questions.hint: Remember that the 24th Amendment was the government's response to the 'transcendental' position given to rights in the late 1960s.

questions.question: If a Constitutional Amendment Bill seeks to change the federal provisions of the Constitution, what is the required ratification from the States?

answerOptions.text: Ratification by at least half of the state legislatures by a simple majority.
answerOptions.rationale: Amendments to federal provisions require ratification by the legislatures of half the states through a simple majority.

answerOptions.text: Ratification by all the state legislatures by a special majority.
answerOptions.rationale: Consent from all states is not required; the Constitution only specifies half, and the majority required at the state level is simple, not special.

answerOptions.text: Ratification by two-thirds of the state legislatures by a simple majority.
answerOptions.rationale: The requirement is specifically half of the states, not a two-thirds majority of states.

answerOptions.text: Ratification by half of the state legislatures by a special majority.
answerOptions.rationale: While the number of states is correct, the legislatures use a simple majority, not the special majority used in Parliament.

questions.hint: Focus on the proportion of states and the specific type of majority required within those state legislatures.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the 'Basic Structure' of the Indian Constitution:
1. The Constitution of India explicitly defines the components of its 'basic structure'.
2. The doctrine was first propounded by the Supreme Court in the Shankari Prasad case (1951).
3. It limits the constituent power of the Parliament under Article 368.

answerOptions.rationale: The doctrine is an evolutionary judicial concept, not defined in the Constitution, and was first laid down in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) to limit parliamentary power.
This is incorrect because the 'basic structure' is nowhere defined in the text of the Constitution.
This incorrectly attributes the origin of the doctrine to the 1951 Shankari Prasad case instead of the 1973 Kesavananda Bharati case.
This is entirely incorrect as it ignores the fact that the doctrine is not defined in the text and was established much later than 1951.

questions.hint: Think about which landmark case in 1973 fundamentally changed the understanding of parliamentary amendment powers.

questions.question: In the context of the Shankari Prasad case (1951), the Supreme Court ruled that the word 'law' in Article 13 includes:

answerOptions.text: Only ordinary laws and not constitutional amendment acts.
answerOptions.rationale: The Court held that Article 368 amendments are constituent powers and do not fall under the definition of 'law' used in Article 13.

answerOptions.text: Both ordinary laws and constitutional amendment acts.
answerOptions.rationale: This view was later adopted in the Golak Nath case, but in Shankari Prasad, the Court differentiated between the two.

answerOptions.text: Only constitutional amendment acts and not ordinary laws.
answerOptions.rationale: This is illogical as Article 13 primarily addresses the validity of ordinary laws passed by legislatures.

answerOptions.text: Neither ordinary laws nor constitutional amendment acts.
answerOptions.rationale: Article 13 clearly applies to ordinary laws; the legal debate specifically concerned whether constitutional amendments were also included.

questions.hint: Recall how the Court distinguished between 'constituent power' and 'legislative power' in the early years of the Republic.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the 'special majority' required in Parliament for a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368?

answerOptions.text: Majority of total strength of the House and a majority of two-thirds of members present and voting.
answerOptions.rationale: Article 368 requires a dual requirement: more than $50\%$ of total membership and at least $2/3$ of those currently participating.

answerOptions.text: A simple majority of the total strength of the House only.
answerOptions.rationale: A simple majority is insufficient for Article 368 amendments; it only applies to non-Article 368 changes.

answerOptions.text: A two-thirds majority of the total strength of the House.
answerOptions.rationale: The $2/3$ requirement applies to those 'present and voting', not the total strength (which only requires more than $50\%$).

answerOptions.text: A majority of members present and voting provided it is at least $25\%$ of total strength.
answerOptions.rationale: The threshold of $25\%$ is incorrect; the Constitution mandates a majority of the total strength ($50\% + 1$).

questions.hint: Think about the two distinct mathematical thresholds that must be met simultaneously.

questions.question: Regarding the President's role in the amendment process, which of the following is true after a bill is passed by both Houses?

answerOptions.text: The President must give his assent and cannot return the bill for reconsideration.
answerOptions.rationale: The source material specifies that the President must give assent and lacks the power to withhold it or send it back for a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

answerOptions.text: The President may exercise a suspensive veto by sending the bill back for reconsideration once.
answerOptions.rationale: While the President can do this for ordinary bills, he is constitutionally obligated to sign amendment bills.

answerOptions.text: The President must obtain the advice of the Supreme Court before giving assent.
answerOptions.rationale: There is no requirement for judicial consultation before signing a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

answerOptions.text: The President has the discretion to withhold assent if the bill violates the basic structure.
answerOptions.rationale: The President has no such discretionary power; the determination of 'basic structure' is a judicial function after the bill becomes law.

questions.hint: Look for the absolute obligation placed on the President once the bill reaches his desk.

questions.question: The Golak Nath case (1967) is significant because the Supreme Court held that Fundamental Rights are:

answerOptions.text: 'Transcendental and immutable' and cannot be abridged by Parliament.
answerOptions.rationale: The Court reversed its earlier stand, giving Fundamental Rights a status that protected them even from constitutional amendments.

answerOptions.text: Subject to the constituent power of the Parliament under Article 368.
answerOptions.rationale: This was the position in Shankari Prasad, but the Golak Nath ruling specifically rejected this.

answerOptions.text: Secondary to the Directive Principles of State Policy.
answerOptions.rationale: The Golak Nath case focused on the immunity of Fundamental Rights from amendment, not their relationship with Directive Principles.

answerOptions.text: Only protected from ordinary laws but not from constitutional amendments.
answerOptions.rationale: The core of the Golak Nath ruling was that amendments are indeed 'laws' under Article 13 and cannot violate Fundamental Rights.

questions.hint: Consider the high status the Court assigned to these rights that made them 'untouchable' by amendment.

questions.question: Which specific Amendment Act was upheld by the Supreme Court in the Kesavananda Bharati case, while simultaneously introducing the Basic Structure doctrine?

answerOptions.rationale: The Court upheld the validity of the 24th Amendment but added the caveat that the 'basic structure' cannot be altered.
The 42nd Amendment was passed in 1976, which is after the 1973 Kesavananda Bharati judgment.
The 1st Amendment was challenged much earlier in the Shankari Prasad case (1951).
The 44th Amendment was passed in 1978, five years after the Kesavananda Bharati case.

questions.hint: Identify the 1971 act that sought to nullify the Golak Nath ruling.

questions.question: According to the source material, what is the nature of the Indian Constitution regarding amendments?

answerOptions.text: A synthesis of both flexibility and rigidity.
answerOptions.rationale: The Constitution is neither purely flexible like Britain's nor purely rigid like the USA's, but a balance of both.

answerOptions.text: Strictly rigid, requiring state consent for all amendments.
answerOptions.rationale: Many amendments can be made by Parliament alone, and some even by simple majority, showing it is not strictly rigid.

answerOptions.text: Completely flexible, allowing Parliament to change any part by simple majority.
answerOptions.rationale: The requirement for special majorities and the 'Basic Structure' doctrine prevent it from being completely flexible.

answerOptions.text: Rigid in terms of Fundamental Rights but flexible in terms of federal provisions.
answerOptions.rationale: Federal provisions actually require a more rigid process (state ratification), while some other parts are easier to change.

questions.hint: Look for a phrase that describes the middle path taken by the Constitution makers.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as an example of the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution in the provided text?

answerOptions.rationale: While 'Supremacy of the Constitution' is a basic feature, 'Parliamentary Sovereignty' is not mentioned and is limited by judicial review.
The text explicitly lists 'Judicial Review' as an example of what constitutes the Basic Structure.
The text explicitly lists 'Supremacy of the Constitution' as an example of what constitutes the Basic Structure.
The text explicitly lists 'Independence of Judiciary' as an example of what constitutes the Basic Structure.

questions.hint: Distinguish between the supremacy of the written document versus the absolute power of the legislature.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
1. Amendments made by a simple majority of Parliament are not deemed constitutional amendments under Article 368.
2. Admission or establishment of new states can be done by a simple majority.

answerOptions.rationale: Certain changes are excluded from the scope of Article 368 even though they amend the text, and these are passed by simple majority.
While statement 1 is correct, statement 2 is also a standard example of a change made outside Article 368.
While statement 2 is correct, statement 1 accurately reflects the technical distinction made in the Constitution regarding Article 368.
Both statements are correct; simple majority amendments are technically excluded from Article 368's specific procedural requirements.

questions.hint: Check the note under 'Types of Amendments' regarding changes that fall outside the formal Article 368 process.

questions.question: The constituent power of Parliament under Article 368 was limited by the Supreme Court to ensure it does not enable the Parliament to:

answerOptions.text: Alter the 'basic structure' of the Constitution.
answerOptions.rationale: The Kesavananda Bharati ruling established that Article 368 does not grant the power to destroy the foundational pillars of the Constitution.

answerOptions.text: Amend the Preamble of the Constitution.
answerOptions.rationale: The Preamble can be amended as long as the basic structure remains intact.

answerOptions.text: Increase the number of judges in the Supreme Court.
answerOptions.rationale: This is an ordinary legislative power and not a limitation imposed by the basic structure doctrine.

answerOptions.text: Legislate on subjects in the State List.
answerOptions.rationale: This is a matter of the division of powers, not a limitation specifically derived from the 'constituent power' under Article 368.

questions.hint: Look for the specific phrase that acts as the ultimate 'ceiling' on Parliament's amending power.

questions.question: Which case reversed the stand taken in the Shankari Prasad case regarding the Parliament's power to take away Fundamental Rights?

answerOptions.rationale: In 1967, the Supreme Court reversed its 1951 position, ruling that Fundamental Rights cannot be abridged.
Kesavananda Bharati actually overruled Golak Nath and partially restored the power to amend rights, though with limits.
This case is not mentioned in the provided source material as the primary reversal of the Shankari Prasad stand.
This was a legislative action, not a court case reversing a previous judicial stand.

questions.hint: Identify the case from the 1960s that created a constitutional crisis by making rights 'immutable'.

questions.question: In the process of constitutional evolution, the 24th Amendment Act (1971) specifically amended which of the following?

answerOptions.rationale: The 24th Amendment aimed to clarify that Article 13 does not apply to amendments made under Article 368.
While it amended Article 368, its primary focus was the relationship with Article 13's definition of 'law'.
It simultaneously amended Article 13 to ensure amendments were not considered 'laws' that could be voided for violating rights.
It amended the procedural and definitional articles (13 and 368) to enable changes to rights, rather than amending specific rights directly.

questions.hint: Focus on the two articles that were at the center of the 'Is an amendment a law?' debate.

questions.question: What happens if there is a disagreement between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha over a Constitutional Amendment Bill?

answerOptions.text: The bill fails to pass as there is no provision for a joint sitting.
answerOptions.rationale: Unlike ordinary bills, the special procedure for amendments requires separate approval; failure to agree means the bill is dead.

answerOptions.text: The Lok Sabha's decision prevails because it represents the people.
answerOptions.rationale: Both Houses are given equal standing in the constitutional amendment process.

answerOptions.text: The President resolves the disagreement through a joint sitting.
answerOptions.rationale: The Constitution specifically excludes the joint sitting mechanism for amendments.

answerOptions.text: The bill is referred to a joint committee of both Houses for mediation.
answerOptions.rationale: The source material states there is 'NO provision for holding a joint sitting', implying no formal mediation mechanism exists to force the bill through.

questions.hint: Think about whether there is any 'safety valve' mechanism mentioned for deadlocks in this procedure.

questions.question:
Match the following terms with their correct descriptions:
A. Synthesis of flexibility and rigidity
B. Simple Majority
C. Special Majority

1. Used for amendments NOT deemed under Article 368
2. Nature of the Indian Constitution
3. Required for amendments under Article 368

answerOptions.rationale: The Constitution is a synthesis, simple majority covers non-Art 368 changes, and special majority is required for Art 368.
This incorrectly matches the nature of the Constitution (Synthesis) with simple majority amendments.
This wrongly suggests Article 368 amendments use a simple majority.
This incorrectly pairs the synthesis of the Constitution with the special majority requirement.

questions.hint: Match the core characteristic of the Constitution with the appropriate majority types mentioned in the text.

questions.question: According to the 'Basic Structure' doctrine, what is the status of the Parliament's power to take away Fundamental Rights?

answerOptions.text: Parliament can take away Fundamental Rights, provided they do not form part of the 'basic structure'.
answerOptions.rationale: The Kesavananda Bharati case ruled that while rights are amendable, those that are core features (basic structure) remain protected.

answerOptions.text: Parliament has absolute power to take away any Fundamental Right under Article 368.
answerOptions.rationale: This was the 24th Amendment's goal, but the Supreme Court qualified it with the Basic Structure doctrine.

answerOptions.text: Parliament cannot take away any Fundamental Rights at all.
answerOptions.rationale: This was the Golak Nath position, which was overruled by the Kesavananda Bharati case.

answerOptions.text: Parliament can only take away Fundamental Rights with the unanimous consent of all states.
answerOptions.rationale: State ratification is only for federal provisions; most Fundamental Rights amendments only require a special majority of Parliament.

questions.hint: Identify the compromise reached in 1973 between absolute parliamentary power and absolute judicial protection of rights.

questions.question: Who determines which features of the Constitution constitute the 'Basic Structure'?

answerOptions.text: The Courts, through an evolutionary process of judicial decisions.
answerOptions.rationale: The doctrine is not written in the Constitution; it is decided and expanded by the judiciary over time.

answerOptions.text: The Parliament, by passing a resolution with a special majority.
answerOptions.rationale: The doctrine acts as a check ON the Parliament, so Parliament cannot define its own limits.

answerOptions.text: The President, in consultation with the Attorney General.
answerOptions.rationale: The executive has no role in defining the basic structure; it is strictly a judicial concept.

answerOptions.text: The Constitution itself, in a dedicated Annexure.
answerOptions.rationale: The source material explicitly states 'Written in Constitution? – NO'.

questions.hint: Reflect on the phrase 'Decided by courts' in the source material.

title: Rights Quiz (Fundamental Rights)

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the definition of 'State' under Article 12:
1. The term includes all local authorities such as Municipalities and Panchayats.
2. Private bodies or companies working as an instrument of the State fall within the meaning of 'State'.
3. The Supreme Court and High Courts are explicitly listed as 'State' under Article 12 of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Article 12 covers executive and legislative organs, local authorities, and statutory bodies, and judicial precedents extend this to private entities acting as state instruments, but superior courts are not explicitly listed.
While the judiciary is bound by the Constitution, the Rupa Ashok Hurra case clarified that Superior Courts do not fall under the explicit scope of Article 12.
This ignores the inclusion of local authorities, which is a foundational part of the definition provided in the text.
This is incomplete because the Supreme Court has interpreted private bodies working as state instruments to also be included.

questions.hint: Think about the specific entities mentioned in Article 12 and the clarification provided by the Rupa Ashok Hurra case.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 13 of the Indian Constitution:
1. It declares that all laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights (FRs) shall be void.
2. A Constitutional Amendment is considered a 'law' within the meaning of Article 13 and cannot be challenged.
3. Non-legislative sources like customs having the force of law are included in the definition of 'law'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Article 13 covers permanent, temporary, and delegated legislation along with customs, but specifically notes that while amendments are not 'laws' under this article, they can still be challenged if they violate FRs.
The text explicitly states that a Constitutional Amendment is NOT a law under Article 13, though it remains challengeable under the Kesavananda Bharati case.
This overlooks the inclusion of customs and non-legislative sources which are validly part of the Article 13 definition.
The second statement is factually incorrect based on the text provided regarding the status of Constitutional Amendments.

questions.hint: Recall the status of Constitutional Amendments after the 1973 Kesavananda Bharati case.

questions.question:
Which of the following Fundamental Rights are available ONLY to the citizens of India and not to foreigners?
1. Article 15 (Prohibition of discrimination)
2. Article 21 (Protection of life and personal liberty)
3. Article 16 (Equality of opportunity in public employment)
4. Article 29 (Protection of language, script and culture)
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

answerOptions.rationale: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 are reserved exclusively for citizens, whereas Article 21 is a universal right available to all persons.
Article 21 is one of the most basic rights available to every person on Indian soil, including foreigners.
Article 2 is actually available to everyone, while Article 15 and 16 are strictly for citizens.
This misses Article 29, which is part of the cultural and educational rights also reserved only for citizens/minorities.

questions.hint: Distinguish between rights aimed at civic participation/identity and those protecting basic human survival.

questions.question: Regarding the exceptions to 'Equality before Law' under Article 14, which of the following statements is NOT correct?

answerOptions.text: Diplomatic immunity from civil and criminal proceedings is only provided to the UNO.
answerOptions.rationale: Immunity is provided to foreign sovereigns, ambassadors, and diplomats in addition to the UNO.

answerOptions.text: No MP shall be liable to any proceedings in court for anything said in Parliament.
answerOptions.rationale: This is a correct statement based on the protections offered by Article 105.

answerOptions.text: Laws giving effect to $Art. 39(b)$ and (c) cannot be challenged for violating Article 14.
answerOptions.rationale: This is a correct legal exception provided under Article 31C.

answerOptions.text: The President and Governors enjoy immunity from criminal proceedings during their term.
answerOptions.rationale: The source material confirms that the President and Governors are exceptions to the general rule of equality under Article 14.

questions.hint: Consider the scope of diplomatic immunity mentioned in the text.

questions.question: Article 15 prohibits discrimination by the State on certain grounds. Identify the ground that is included in Article 16 but NOT in Article 15:

answerOptions.rationale: Article 15 lists five grounds (religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth), while Article 16 adds descent and residence for public employment matters.
Both Article 15 and 16 include religion and race as prohibited grounds of discrimination.
Caste and sex are common prohibited grounds for both Article 15 and Article 16.
Place of birth is listed in both articles, though Article 16 expands the list further.

questions.hint: Check the list of grounds for public employment versus general social discrimination.

questions.question:
With reference to the 'Abolition of Titles' under Article 18, consider the following statements:
1. The State is prohibited from conferring any title, including military or academic distinctions.
2. An Indian citizen is prohibited from accepting any title from any foreign state.
3. National Awards like Bharat Ratna are considered 'titles' within the meaning of Article 18.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Military and academic distinctions are exempted from the prohibition, and the Supreme Court has ruled that National Awards do not amount to titles.
Statement 1 is incorrect because military and academic distinctions are specifically allowed as exceptions.
Statement 3 is incorrect as the source explicitly states National Awards do not amount to titles.
The presence of military/academic exceptions and the status of National Awards make statements 1 and 3 false.

questions.hint: Identify the specific exceptions allowed for the State to confer distinctions.

questions.question:
Arrange the following events related to Fundamental Rights in correct chronological order:
1. Deletion of the Right to Property from Part III.
2. Introduction of the Right to Education as a Fundamental Right.
3. Institution of Padma Awards.
4. Addition of 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS).
Select the correct sequence:

answerOptions.rationale: Padma Awards (1954), 44th Amendment (1978), 86th Amendment (2002), and 103rd Amendment (2019) is the correct historical sequence.
The Padma awards were instituted in 1954, much earlier than the 44th Amendment of 1978.
The deletion of the property right (1978) occurred before the addition of the education right (2002).
This sequence fails to place the institution of awards (1954) at the beginning of the timeline.

questions.hint: The Right to Property was removed in the late 70s, while EWS is a very recent addition.

questions.question: Which of the following protections is NOT granted under Article 20 in respect of conviction for offences?

answerOptions.text: Protection against self-incrimination in civil and tax proceedings.
answerOptions.rationale: The text notes that ex-post-facto protections only apply to criminal laws, and double jeopardy does not apply to administrative authorities; similarly, the specific protections are criminal in nature.

answerOptions.text: Protection against Double Jeopardy in judicial proceedings.
answerOptions.rationale: This is a correct protection explicitly mentioned as being part of Article 20.

answerOptions.text: Protection against Ex-post-facto laws regarding criminal legislation.
answerOptions.rationale: This is one of the three core protections listed under Article 20 in the source.

answerOptions.text: Protection against compulsory production of thumb impressions.
answerOptions.rationale: The text states that self-incrimination protection DOES NOT extend to thumb impressions, making this a validly excluded item.

questions.hint: Check if Article 20 protections extend to civil matters or administrative proceedings.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 21 and the Maneka Case (1978):
1. It overruled the narrow interpretation of the Gopalan Case (1950).
2. It established that a law depriving life or liberty must be reasonable, fair, and just.
3. It introduced the concept of 'Procedure Established by Law' for the first time in India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: The Maneka case overruled Gopalan by requiring 'fair' procedure (moving toward due process), whereas 'Procedure Established by Law' was already in the text of Article 21 since its inception.
Statement 3 is wrong because the phrase 'Procedure Established by Law' is the original constitutional text, not a Maneka case innovation.
While statement 2 is correct, statement 1 is also a critical part of the Maneka case's historical significance.
Statement 3 misattributes the origin of the constitutional phrase to the 1978 case.

questions.hint: The Maneka case changed the *interpretation* of existing text rather than adding new phrases to the Constitution.

questions.question: With reference to the 'Right to Education' under Article 21A, which of the following is correct?

answerOptions.text: The State must provide free and compulsory education only to children aged six to fourteen.
answerOptions.rationale: The text specifies the age group of 6 to 14 years and clarifies that only elementary education is a fundamental right.

answerOptions.text: It includes the right to higher and professional education.
answerOptions.rationale: The source explicitly states that only elementary education is a fundamental right, not higher education.

answerOptions.text: It was added to the Constitution by the 44th Amendment Act of 1978.
answerOptions.rationale: The text attributes the addition of Article 21A to the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002.

questions.question:

3. The detenu must be afforded an opportunity to make a representation against the detention order.

answerOptions.rationale: Grounds should be communicated, but the text notes an exception where facts against public interest need not be disclosed.
Statement 2 is false because public interest allows the State to withhold certain facts.

questions.hint: Look for a specific exception related to 'public interest' in the communication of grounds.

questions.question:
Which of the following is specifically prohibited under the 'Right against Exploitation' (Articles 23-24)?
1. Begar (forced labour without remuneration).
2. Employment of children below 14 years in harmless household work.
3. Compulsory service for public purposes imposed by the State.
4. Selling and buying of women and children.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

answerOptions.rationale: Begar and trafficking are prohibited, but child labor is only prohibited in hazardous activities, and the State can impose compulsory public service.
Article 24 does not prohibit children's employment in harmless or innocent work.
The State is permitted to impose compulsory service for public purposes as an exception to Article 23.
These two items are actually permitted under the specific exceptions or narrow scopes defined in the text.

questions.hint: Identify the exceptions related to 'harmless work' and 'public purposes'.

questions.question:
Match the following types of educational institutions with their permissible religious instruction under Article 28:
1. Wholly maintained by State - (P) Voluntary basis

answerOptions.rationale: The text states instruction is prohibited in wholly-maintained schools (Q), permitted in trust-established ones (R), and voluntary in recognized ones (P).

This sequence completely reverses the prohibitions and permissions stated in the source.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding 'Minority Rights' under Articles 29 and 30:
1. Article 29 is limited only to religious and linguistic minorities.
2. Article 30 grants the right to establish educational institutions to all 'sections of citizens'.

answerOptions.rationale: Article 29 applies to 'any section of citizens' (including majorities), while Article 30 is exclusive to minorities. Neither defines the term 'minority'.
Statement 1 is false because Article 29 uses the broader phrase 'any section of the citizens'.
Statement 2 is false as Article 30 rights are available ONLY to minorities, unlike Article 29.
The distinct scopes of Article 29 (any section) and Article 30 (minorities only) make statements 1 and 2 incorrect.

questions.hint: Differentiate between the 'section of citizens' mentioned in Article 29 and the 'minorities' mentioned in Article 30.

questions.question: Which of the following features of Fundamental Rights (FRs) is correct based on the provided material?

answerOptions.text: Some FRs are negative in character as they place limitations on the authority of the State.
answerOptions.rationale: The text explicitly defines some rights as negative (limits on State) and others as positive (privileges to persons).

answerOptions.text: Fundamental Rights are sacrosanct and cannot be amended by Parliament.
answerOptions.rationale: The source clarifies that FRs are NOT sacrosanct and Parliament can curtail or repeal them (without affecting basic structure).

answerOptions.text: All Fundamental Rights are suspended automatically during a National Emergency.

questions.question: According to the source material, why are Fundamental Rights termed as 'fundamental'?

answerOptions.text: They are guaranteed by the fundamental law of the land and are essential for all-round development.

answerOptions.text: They were inspired by the Magna Carta of the United Kingdom.

answerOptions.text: They promote the ideals of social and economic democracy.
answerOptions.rationale: The text specifically states that Fundamental Rights promote the ideals of POLITICAL democracy.

answerOptions.rationale: The source explicitly says FRs are 'Not absolute but qualified'.

questions.question: Regarding the scope of Article 14, what is the effect of Article 31C as mentioned in the text?

answerOptions.text: It provides the Supreme Court the power to issue writs.
answerOptions.rationale: The writ-issuing power is provided by Article 32.

answerOptions.text: It exempts the President and Governor from civil proceedings.

questions.question: Which specific Fundamental Right was moved to Article 300A after the 44th Amendment?

answerOptions.rationale: The source material clearly marks that the Right to property (Article 31) was moved to $Art. 300A$ by the 44th Amendment.
The Right to education was added to Part III much later by the 86th Amendment, not moved out.

questions.question: With reference to Article 19, which of the following is NOT one of the six protected freedoms?

answerOptions.text: Freedom to acquire and dispose of property.
answerOptions.rationale: The source states that the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property was deleted from Article 19 by the 44th Amendment in 1978.

questions.question: What is the primary aim of Fundamental Rights according to the provided material?

answerOptions.text: To ensure a government of laws and not of men.

questions.question:

questions.question: Regarding the nature and scope of Fundamental Duties, which of the following statements is correct according to the provided material?

answerOptions.text: They extend to both citizens and foreigners residing in India.
answerOptions.rationale: Fundamental Duties are explicitly confined to citizens only and do not apply to aliens.

answerOptions.text: They serve as a guide for the courts in determining the constitutional validity of a law.

answerOptions.text: They consist exclusively of moral duties related to Indian tradition.

questions.question: Which of the following is categorized as a 'Civic Duty' under Article $51A$?

questions.question:

questions.question:

questions.question: Which of the following Fundamental Duties was added to the Constitution by the $86^{th}$ Amendment Act of $2002$?
